roles: formal, summary | topics: t-tests, hypothesis-tests, paired-data
synopsis: Presents the complete procedure for a hypothesis test about a population mean: identify the one-sample t-test, parameter, significance level, and hypotheses; check independence and normality conditions; calculate the t-statistic, df, and p-value; and conclude by comparing the p-value to α. Notes that paired numerical data use the same procedure to test whether the mean population difference µd is zero, using the mean and standard deviation of sample differences.
To carry out a complete hypothesis test to evaluate a claim about a population mean, Identify: Identify the test procedure, parameter, signiﬁcance level, and hypotheses.

Use a one-sample t-test for a population mean µ. Deﬁne the population mean µ in words, referencing the population of interest. Choose a signiﬁcance level (α) and test the following hypotheses.

H0: µ = µ0 HA: µ ≠ µ0; µ > µ0; or µ < µ0 (µ0 is the null or hypothesized mean)

When there is paired numerical data, use this same procedure to test whether µd, the mean of the population diﬀerences, is zero. In this case, use the mean and standard deviation of the sample diﬀerences, x¯d and sd, and the number of sample diﬀerences, nd, when calculating the test statistic.

Check: Check conditions for the test statistic to have a t-distribution, assuming H0 is true.

1. Independence: Data come from a random sample or random process. When sampling without replacement, check that sample size is less than 10% of the population size.
2. Large sample or normal population: n ≥ 30 or the population distribution is nearly normal. If the sample size is less than 30 and the population distribution is unknown, check and conﬁrm that there is no strong skew or outliers in the data in order to reasonably assume that the population distribution is nearly normal.

Calculate: Calculate the t-statistic, df, and p-value.

T = point SEestimateof estimate− null value, df = n − 1 point estimate: x¯, the sample mean SE of estimate: √sn null value: µ0

roles: worked_example, reference | topics: paired-data, t-tests, jamovi | figures: fig_45ecdb7da7734b_1979_v2, fig_45ecdb7da7734b_1981_v2
synopsis: Describes doing a paired samples t-test in jamovi, either by creating a difference variable and running a one sample t-test, or by using the jamovi 'Paired Samples T-Test' analysis. Reports an average improvement of 1.4% from test 1 to test 2, significantly different from 0 (t(19) = 6.48, p < .001). Notes the paired samples t-test is a one sample test under the hood, so results are identical.
How do you do a paired samples 𝑡-test in jamovi? One possibility is to follow the process I outlined above. That is, create a “difference” variable and then run a one sample 𝑡-test on that. Since we’ve already created a variable called “improvement”, let’s do that and see what we get, Figure 11.15.

Figure 11.15. Results showing a one sample 𝑡-test on paired difference scores The output shown in Figure 11.15 is (obviously) formatted exactly the same was as it was the last time we used the one-sample 𝑡-test analysis (Section 11.2), and it confirms our intuition. There’s an average improvement of 1.4% from test 1 to test 2, and this is significantly different from 0 (𝑡(19) = 6.48,𝑝 < .001). However, suppose you’re lazy and you don’t want to go to all the effort of creating a new variable. Or perhaps you just want to keep the difference between one-sample and paired samples tests clear in your head. If so, you can use the jamovi ‘Paired Samples T-Test’ analysis, getting the results shown in Figure 11.16.
Figure 11.16. Results showing a paired sample 𝑡-test. Compare with Figure 11.15

The numbers are identical to those that come from the one sample test, which of course they have to be given that the paired samples 𝑡-test is just a one sample test under the hood.

roles: reference, formal | topics: t-tests, paired-data, hypothesis-tests
synopsis: Provides calculator steps for performing a one-sample t-test and summarizes the procedure: hypotheses H0: µ = µ0 with one- or two-sided alternatives, conditions (independence; n ≥ 30 or nearly normal population), test statistic T = (x̄ − µ0)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1, p-value interpretation, and formal decision comparing p-value to α. Notes that matched pairs designs use a one-sample t-test on differences with µd, x̄d, sd, and nd.
• The appropriate hypothesis testing procedure for a population mean µ with unknown population standard deviation σ is a one-sample t-test for a population mean µ. The parameter µ should be identiﬁed in context.
• For a matched pairs design, the appropriate analysis calculates diﬀerences between pairs of values to produce one sample of diﬀerences. The hypothesis testing procedure for a matched pairs design is a one-sample t-test for a population mean diﬀerence, where we use µd for the population mean diﬀerence, x¯d for the mean of sample diﬀerences, sd for the standard deviation of sample diﬀerences, and nd for the number of sample diﬀerences.
• The null hypotheses for a one-sample t-test for a population mean µ is: H0: µ = µ0, where µ0 is the null hypothesized value for the population mean.
• The alternative hypothesis may be one-sided (< or >) or two-sided (≠). HA: µ < µ0. The p-value will correspond to a lower tail. HA: µ > µ0. The p-value will correspond to an upper tail. HA: µ ≠ µ0. The p-value will correspond to both tails.
• The one-sample t-test for a population mean or mean diﬀerence has the same conditions as the one-sample t-interval. We check that the following conditions are met. 1. Independence: The data come from a random sample or random process. When sampling without replacement, check that the sample size is less than 10% of the population size. 2. Large sample or normal population: n ≥ 30 or population distribution is nearly normal.

title: Paired-Samples t-Test: Concept and Worked Example
content:
# Paired-Samples t-Test

## What it is
A paired-samples t-test compares the **means of two measurements taken from the same units** (e.g., the same people before and after a treatment, or matched pairs). Because the two observations are dependent, you don't compare the two samples directly — you reduce the data to **one sample of difference scores** and run an ordinary **one-sample t-test** on them.

## Setup
For each pair *i*, compute the difference score:

- **D_i = X_i1 − X_i2** (variable 1 minus variable 2 — pick the order so that the effect you expect gets a positive sign)
- **μ_D = μ_1 − μ_2** is the population mean difference

## Hypotheses (two-sided)
- H₀: μ_D = 0 (no average change)
- H₁: μ_D ≠ 0 (one-sided versions: μ_D > 0 or μ_D < 0)

## Test statistic
With D̄ = mean of the difference scores, σ̂_D = their standard deviation, and N = number of pairs:

**t = D̄ / (σ̂_D / √N)**, with **df = N − 1**

Conditions: the pairs are independent of each other (random sampling), and the difference scores are roughly normal (or N is large, ~30+).

## Worked example: test 1 vs test 2 (N = 20 students)
Each student takes the same test twice; we want to know whether scores improved.

1. **Difference scores:** D_i = test 2 − test 1 for each of the 20 students, so improvement corresponds to a positive D.
2. **Hypotheses:** H₀: μ_D = 0 vs H₁: μ_D ≠ 0.
3. **Result:** the mean improvement is D̄ = 1.4% (with σ̂_D/√N giving SE ≈ 0.22).
4. **Statistic:** t = 1.4 / 0.22 ≈ **6.48**, df = 20 − 1 = **19**.
5. **Decision:** p < .001, so reject H₀ at α = .05 — there is strong evidence of a genuine average improvement of 1.4% from test 1 to test 2.

Running a one-sample t-test on the "improvement" variable and running a dedicated paired-samples t-test give **identical numbers** — the paired test is just a one-sample test under the hood.

## Why not an independent-samples t-test?
Same-unit measurements are correlated; the paired test removes the between-person variability by working with differences, giving a more powerful (smaller-SE) test when pairing is genuine. Use the independent test only when the two groups contain different, unrelated units.

answer:
Done — I created the study note **"Paired-Samples t-Test: Concept and Worked Example"** (mat_4770957888fed352).

It covers, concisely:
- **What the test is:** a one-sample t-test applied to difference scores from paired measurements (D_i = X_i1 − X_i2, μ_D = μ_1 − μ_2).
- **Hypotheses and statistic:** H₀: μ_D = 0, t = D̄ / (σ̂_D/√N) with df = N − 1, plus the conditions (independent pairs, roughly normal differences).
- **Worked example:** 20 students tested twice — mean improvement of 1.4%, t(19) = 6.48, p < .001, rejecting H₀.
- **Why pairing beats an independent-samples test** when the same units are measured twice.

It's built from *Learning Statistics with R* (formal treatment of difference scores) and *Learning Statistics with jamovi* (the worked example and software results).
